task: Cuenta en 80–100 palabras una entrevista, un examen oral o una prueba importante que hayas tenido: cómo te preparaste, qué pasó y qué aprendiste. Usa el pasado simple y el past perfect.
paragraphs: I was twenty-two when I applied for my first proper job, as an assistant in a small design studio. I had sent out more than forty applications, so when the studio finally called me, I was thrilled and terrified at the same time.

The night before the interview, I prepared answers to all the typical questions: Why do you want this job? What are your strengths and weaknesses? Where do you see yourself in five years? I even practised in front of the mirror. I chose my clothes carefully and set three alarms.

Of course, the day did not go as planned. My bus broke down halfway, and I had to run the last two kilometres. I arrived ten minutes late, out of breath, with my shirt stuck to my back. The receptionist smiled kindly and offered me a glass of water.

The interview itself was nothing like the one I had imagined. The manager, a calm woman called Priya, did not ask a single question from my list. Instead, she showed me a poster and asked me what I would change. I was nervous, but I explained my ideas honestly. Then she asked about a mistake I had made at university and what I had learned from it.

Two days later, Priya phoned to offer me the job. Months afterwards, I asked her why she had chosen me, even though I had arrived late. "You apologised, you didn't make excuses, and you told me what you really thought about the poster," she said. "Skills can be taught. Honesty is harder."
Since then, I have been on the other side of the table many times. My advice is simple: prepare, but don't learn a script. Interviewers want to meet a person, not a recording.
